failure_summary.description: Wrong answer class for the clue's category noun. The agent gave the event instead of 'this Crimean city' (Yalta Conference), a base instead of 'this very caustic acid' (caustic soda), and the energy restated instead of its source for 'the energy from this' (direct solar radiation).
The clue gave the middle name, and the agent spelled it out ('Warren Gamaliel Harding'). The key uses the initial form ('Warren G. Harding').

Bare definition fragments or 'seen here' clues. The agent picked a neighbouring role (Curate for 'Anglican parish priest', which the passages call a vicar or rector) or the most famous brand item (Twinkie) instead of the generic term that fits every defining word (cupcake).
The (4) letter-count rule and its example were in the skill, but the agent answered a 6-letter word (FLOOSIE) instead of 'Moll'.
A bare 'person + for adultery' fragment whose hidden category answer was an era ('the 19th century'). It is not inferable from the passages.

patch.reasoning: Three of eight failures are class errors, where the answer is a related entity rather than a member of the clue's category noun. Prior large 'Step 0' prepends were rejected, so I add short, targeted bullets. One goes next to the existing category check in Rule 2, with analogue examples so no gold answers are embedded. One covers the name form when the clue supplies a middle name. One covers bare definition and 'seen here' fragments, where agents drift to a neighbouring role or a famous brand. I skipped the letter-count and hidden-category cases: the first rule is already explicit and was ignored, and the second is not inferable from the passages.

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content: - CLASS TEST: read the noun after 'this' (with its adjectives) as the class the answer must belong to, and check that your candidate is an instance of that class before answering. 'the 1815 battle in this Belgian town' -> the town ('Waterloo'), not the event ('Battle of Waterloo'). 'this strong acid used in car batteries' -> an acid ('sulfuric acid'); a base or other chemical is the wrong class. 'The energy from this' / 'a product of this' -> the SOURCE or maker (the Sun, a factory), not the energy or product restated in other words. After the class is right, strip any word the clue already states.

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - When the clue itself supplies part of a person's name ('His middle name was Fitzgerald'), do not spell that part out in the answer. Give the usual full-name form with it reduced to an initial, as a trivia key prints it: 'John F. Kennedy', not 'John Fitzgerald Kennedy'.

- Bare definition fragments (a noun phrase with no 'this', e.g. 'A church official who ...', 'a snack cake seen here split in half'): answer with the plain generic common noun that exactly fits the definition, using the term the passages gloss it with ('the head of a school, usually called the principal' -> Principal). Check every defining word and pick the described role or class, not a neighbouring one (an assistant or junior role, a related product, or the most famous brand item). For 'seen here' clues no picture is available, so prefer the generic type name whose passage text pairs the clue's own distinctive phrase (such as 'split in half') with the product, rather than a brand name.
